articles.title: Um ano depois, fraude do Banco Master deixou prejuízo de R$ 76 bilhões | G1
articles.standfirst: Primeira prisão de Daniel Vorcaro e liquidação do Master em novembro de 2025 expuseram vasto esquema de fraudes e tentáculos do banqueiro nos Três Poderes.
articles.summary: Primeira prisão de Daniel Vorcaro e liquidação do Master em novembro de 2025 expuseram vasto esquema de fraudes e tentáculos do banqueiro nos Três Poderes.
articles.body:
Fachada do Banco Master no Itaim Bibi, na Zona Sul de São Paulo, no dia 19 de novembro de 2025 — Foto: Rovena Rosa/Agência Brasil

Na tarde de 18 de novembro de 2025, o Banco Central anunciou a decretação da liquidação extrajudicial do Banco Master e de várias instituições ligadas ao banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro — que havia sido preso na noite anterior no aeroporto de Guarulhos ao tentar embarcar para o Oriente Médio.

Era o fim da trajetória de quase oito anos de Vorcaro como banqueiro e de uma instituição que havia atraído centenas de milhares de clientes por meio do oferecimento Certificados de Depósito Bancário (CDBs) com remunerações bem acima das praticadas por grandes bancos .

Quando teve sua operação encerrada, o Banco Master, uma instituição que no papel contava com mais R$ 90 bilhões em ativos , tinha apenas R$ 4 milhões em caixa.

Mas a liquidação do Master e a primeira prisão de Vorcaro marcariam apenas o começo da revelação da escala das fraudes executadas pela instituição bancária, que ainda teria forte impacto no mundo político e no Judiciário, expondo a cooptação de autoridades por Vorcaro.

Um ano depois, a quebra do Master deixou um rastro de prejuízos que soma R$ 76 bilhões.

Não foi apenas o Master que teve liquidação determinada pelo BC. De 21 liquidações extrajudiciais decretadas pelo órgão em 2026, 11 envolveram instituições ligadas a Vorcaro ou a pessoas do seu círculo , como o Will Bank, a antiga Reag e o Banco Pleno. A liquidação extrajudicial é uma medida previstas pelo BC quando uma instituição financeira é considerada irrecuperável ou quando há constatação de violações contra o sistema financeiro.

O colapso do Master e de instituições satélites de Vorcaro também resultou na maior operação da história do Fundo Garantidor de Créditos (FGC), mecanismo mantido por contribuições de instituições associadas.

O crescimento exponencial do Master havia sido alavancado pela emissão de CDBs, que são cobertos pelo FGC, que garante ressarcimento de até R$ 250 mil por CPF ou CNPJ, por conglomerado financeiro. O esquema do Master justamente fazia um uso sistemático do FGC como chamariz para convencer clientes a investir em títulos do banco, induzindo-os a acreditar que eram de baixo risco.

E a maior parte da fatura da liquidação do Master acabou ficando justamente com o FGC. O fundo já teve que desembolsar R$ 54,8 bilhões para cobrir o prejuízo do esquema fraudulento liderado por Vorcaro.

Deste valor, cerca de R$ 50 bilhões foram direcionados após a quebra do banco e de empresas associadas a Vorcaro, como o Banco Master de Investimento e o Will Bank. Outros R$ 4,3 bilhões já haviam sido usados no primeiro semestre de 2025, quando o Master ainda operava.

Só no caso do Banco Master, os desembolsos chegaram a R$ 28,8 bilhões, distribuídos para cerca de 570,5 mil credores. No total, o FGC já direcionou pagamentos para mais de 1 milhão de credores de empresas do Grupo Master.

Como o fundo é mantido em sua maioria com recursos de grandes bancos, na prática a conta foi em grande parte bancada por instituições mais longevas como o Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, entre outros. Posteriormente, investigações levantaram a suspeita que a tentativa de compra do Master pela cúpula do Banco de Brasília (BRB) foi movida pelo pagamento de dezenas de milhões de reais em propinas por parte de Vorcaro.

O esquema também provocou prejuízos para o BRB, instituição estatal do Distrito Federal que agora busca provisionar R$ 8,8 bilhões para cobrir perdas com carteiras fraudulentas do Master. A proximidade do BRB com o Master foi justamente um dos primeiros sinais de que havia algo errado com o banco de Vorcaro. O próprio BRB tentou adquirir o Master no primeiro semestre de 2025 , numa operação que foi barrada pelo BC.

Regimes de previdência de servidores estaduais e municipais que compraram CDBs e papéis do grupo Master, e que não contavam com garantia do FGC, perderam mais de R$ 4 bilhões. Só o Rioprevidência, fundo de previdência dos servidores do governo do Rio de Janeiro, tinha quase R$ 1 bilhão em aplicações no Master.

O mesmo ocorreu com empresas com títulos do Master, como a Companhia Estadual de Águas e Esgotos do Rio de Janeiro (Cedae), que somaram perdas de cerca de R$ 2,2 bilhões.

Tentáculos no mundo político e no Judiciário

A quebra do Master e a prisão do Vorcaro também expuseram que o banqueiro desenvolveu uma ampla e suspeita rede de relações com membros dos três Poderes, incluindo dirigentes de órgão públicos, integrantes do Congresso Nacional , políticos de diferentes matizes políticas e até ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) . A rede ainda se estendia a fundos de pensão de estados e municípios.

Investigações levantaram suspeitas sobre pagamentos, viagens, encontros, contratos com pessoas próximas a autoridades, possíveis informações privilegiadas e articulações políticas em defesa dos interesses do Banco Master.

No Congresso Nacional , aparecem nomes como Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI), senador e ex-ministro da Casa Civil, que mantinha relação próxima com Vorcaro; Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), presidente da Câmara, mencionado em conversas e articulações envolvendo o banqueiro; Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP), presidente do Senado , citado no contexto das relações políticas; e Fábio Faria (PP-RN), ex-ministro das Comunicações.

O senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que está nos EUA, também passou a ser investigado no contexto do Master, após a revelação de que o político de extrema direita negociou repasses de dezenas de milhões de reais diretamente com Vorcaro.

No STF , Alexandre de Moraes aparece em registros de contatos com Vorcaro, enquanto sua esposa, Viviane Barci de Moraes, manteve contrato de R$ 131 milhões com o Banco Master. Dias Toffoli teve seu nome associado a negócios envolvendo o resort Tayayá e fundos relacionados ao universo empresarial do banqueiro.

Também surgiram questionamentos envolvendo Kassio Nunes Marques, após notícias sobre pagamentos ao advogado Kevin Marques, seu filho; e Luiz Fux, cujo filho, Rodrigo Fux, manteve conversas e contatos próximos com Vorcaro. André Mendonça também recebeu o banqueiro em reunião articulada por intermediários.

No Banco Central, órgão responsável pela fiscalização do sistema financeiro, as suspeitas atingiram Paulo Sérgio Neves de Souza, ex-diretor de Fiscalização, e Belline Santana, ex-chefe do Departamento de Supervisão Bancária, ambos afastados em meio a investigações sobre possíveis pagamentos e favorecimento ao Master.

Vorcaro segue preso atualmente no 19º Batalhão da Polícia Militar no Distrito Federal, a Papudinha.

articles.title: Gold drops from Rs 1.8 lakh high to Rs 1.31 lakh per 10 grams, yet ETF inflows beat 2025's total as investors buy the dip and build exposure through SIPs and lump-sum buys
articles.summary: Gold prices have been crashing but investors’ appetite for gold ETFs or Exchange Traded Funds remains strong.
articles.body: Gold prices have been crashing but investors’ appetite for gold ETFs or Exchange Traded Funds remains strong. Gold prices have fallen by more than 25% since climbing to a record Rs 1.8 lakh per 10 gm in January, giving investors an opportunity to increase their exposure to the precious metal at lower prices.The demand for gold exchange-traded funds has remained robust. The category attracted around Rs 49,399 crore between January and October 2026, exceeding the Rs 42,961 crore it collected during the whole of calendar year 2025.Why gold ETFs are in demandWealth managers say investors are taking advantage of the correction to add gold to their portfolios, either by making lump-sum purchases or investing gradually through weekly or monthly systematic investment plans (SIPs). The staggered approach also helps them average their purchase costs amid continued price volatility.In October, gold ETFs recorded net inflows of approximately Rs 3,474 crore. Although this was lower than the record Rs 4,451 crore received in September, inflows remained significantly above historical averages, extending the run of strong investor demand for gold-backed funds, according to an ET report.On Wednesday, MCX Gold is trading at around Rs 1.31 lakh per 10 grams.The latest decline has been driven by factors such as a stronger US dollar, rising bond yields and uncertainty surrounding the US interest-rate outlook. However, experts believe investors with a long-term investment horizon can use the price dip to build their gold holdings in stages instead of trying to identify the market bottom.“Gold prices have remained under pressure due to less supportive macro factors, including higher yields, a stronger dollar and rate hikes by central banks,” said Tapan Patel, fund manager, commodities, Tata Asset Management. “The current correction provides an opportunity for investors to rebalance their portfolios and add gold as part of their strategic asset allocation.”Patel believes the long-term investment case for gold remains strong. Purchases by central banks, efforts to diversify away from the US dollar, geopolitical tensions and the possibility of a decline in the dollar's value could continue to provide support to prices.Manav Modi of Motilal Oswal Financial Services told the financial daily that shifting expectations about US monetary policy under the new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, have also contributed to the recent correction in gold prices.Gold in free fallGold prices dropped almost 2% on Wednesday, touching their lowest level in more than a year as a stronger US dollar and expectations of higher interest rates weighed on the metal. Investors were also waiting for the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s latest meeting for indications of its future monetary policy.Spot gold was down 1.9% at $3,777.83 an ounce as of 0627 GMT, after slipping to its weakest level since September 2025 earlier in the session. US gold futures for December delivery also declined, losing 2.2% to $3,779.50."The bearish movement in gold prices have been primarily driven by sentiment and technicality, with hawkish reaffirmation from Fed officials and a push up in the US Treasury yields in turn leading to a firmer US dollar," Kelvin Wong, senior market analyst at OANDA was quoted as saying by Reuters.The dollar remained close to a 19-month peak, making gold priced in the US currency costlier for buyers using other currencies.Market participants are now looking to the minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee’s October 27-28 meeting for further clues on the Fed’s policy direction.(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO: How to buy shares, expected price and risks investors should know
articles.summary: AI giant Anthropic is preparing for its stock market debut, giving individual investors an opportunity to own a stake in the company behind chatbot Claude.
articles.body: AI giant Anthropic is preparing for its stock market debut, giving individual investors an opportunity to own a stake in the company behind chatbot Claude. The initial public offering (IPO) is expected to value the company at $1.4 trillion (£1 trillion), making it one of the biggest stock market listings in history.Investor demand is already strong, with reports suggesting that the offering is nearly six times oversubscribed. However, the IPO comes amid volatility in US markets, particularly technology stocks.Here is what investors need to know about the share price, application process and risks before deciding whether to invest.Anthropic IPO priceAccording to the company's prospectus, Anthropic is offering 825 million shares of Class A common stock at an initial price range of $70 to $78 per share. The final price will be decided on Wednesday.The shares will carry voting rights, but all the votes combined will account for only 49.9% of the total voting power. This means investors will not have enough voting rights to force changes in how the company is run.The shares are scheduled to list on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday. Both individual investors and large institutions will be able to participate.How can retail investors apply?Investors in the UK can subscribe to Anthropic shares through AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro. The minimum investment differs across platforms.Robinhood and eToro require a minimum investment of $250 (£189), while Hargreaves Lansdown has set the minimum at £250. AJ Bell requires at least £1,000.The application deadlines are 1pm on Wednesday for AJ Bell and 3pm for Hargreaves Lansdown and Robinhood. All three platforms have warned that applications could close earlier without notice.Those who miss the IPO can still buy shares once they begin trading on the Nasdaq. They will also be available through platforms that are not participating in the offering.Buying Anthropic through mutual fundsDirect investment is not the only way to gain exposure to Anthropic. Some funds already hold stakes in the company.In the UK, these include the Baillie Gifford US Growth and Scottish Mortgage investment trusts. Fidelity also has investments in funds available to US investors.After the listing, Anthropic shares are expected to enter some tracker funds, although the timing will vary. Actively managed funds may also choose to buy the stock. This means investors could gain exposure through their existing fund investments without purchasing shares directly.RisksStrong demand does not necessarily mean the shares will deliver lasting returns. Anthropic's prospectus includes 92 pages detailing potential risks to the company and its industry. Recent volatility in US markets, particularly technology stocks, is another factor investors need to consider.The company's governance structure has also attracted scrutiny. The Guardian's financial editor Nils Pratley has raised concerns, saying it “represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals”.Jason Hollands, managing director of investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners, which is not participating in the IPO, has also highlighted concerns about the company's profitability.“Anthropic would give most retail investors the first opportunity to have a direct stake in a frontier AI developer. But it remains a capital-intensive business, and it has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability,” he told The Guardian. “Investors will need to judge whether the company can turn demand for its models into durable earnings.”Hollands says strong demand and limited share supply could push up the stock initially, but that does not guarantee sustained gains.(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India)Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: No 24x7 trading in immediate future, Sebi chief flags cyber risks, liquidity concerns
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has no immediate plans to introduce round-the-clock stock market trading, with chairman Tuhin
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has no immediate plans to introduce round-the-clock stock market trading, with chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey flagging cybersecurity threats, fragmented liquidity and investor fatigue as key concerns. He said that extending market hours would require a strong justification, given the costs and operational risks involved.Speaking to the media on Wednesday on the sidelines of the 65th General Assembly and Annual Meeting of the World Federation of Exchanges (WFE), Pandey said tha the regulator needs to carefully weigh the potential risks before considering a shift to 24x7 trading."For the 24x7 approach, we should have a very strong kind of reason why should we do it, and what are the costs and what are the risks of that," Pandey told ANI. "Nobody has a clue of how they are going to handle the cybersecurity. Every day something is happening in the US."While he did not comment on extending existing trading hours, Pandey questioned whether longer sessions would necessarily improve market efficiency, pointing to their possible impact on liquidity and retail investors."People will complain that the prices have gone up at night while they were sleeping. Extending the market hours is not necessarily a very efficient way," he said.He also indicated that prediction markets were not a priority for the regulator.Equity tokenisation not feasible for nowOn distributed ledger technology (DLT), Pandey said corporate bond tokenisation was progressing through a three-phase pilot. However, extending the technology to equities was not viable at present because of the scale of India's equity market and the costs involved."Equity is a slightly different cup of tea," he said. "We have to see the efficiency of DLT technologies vis-a-vis equity market cap. DLT cannot handle it, and it will be a very costly technology."Dual listing faces structural hurdlesPandey also highlighted two challenges to allowing Indian companies to list overseas: the absence of full rupee capital account convertibility and India's client-level segregation framework.India tracks individual investors through millions of accounts and around 1,000 clearing members. This differs from markets using omnibus accounts, where clearing corporations have limited visibility into individual end-clients. Aligning the two systems would involve technological challenges, he said."Dual listing would mean that your prices will simply equalize, and all kinds of investors should be capable of trading in all kinds of places," Pandey said.SEBI reviews key market regulationsOn other reforms, Pandey said Sebi was undertaking a comprehensive review of its Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR), Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR), and Innovators Growth Platform (IGP) norms, last overhauled in 2018.The regulator is also examining proposals concerning the Margin Trading Facility (MTF) and a pre-IPO platform.On Securities Lending and Borrowing (SLBM), Pandey said India would follow an exchange-traded model instead of opaque over-the-counter practices."We don't want anything dark pool or outside OTC kind of thing. We want it on exchanges," he said, emphasising the need for transparent market frameworks.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: C-CAMP, French biotech cluster Genopole sign Indo-French collaboration pact
articles.summary: BENGALURU: In a move to strengthen cross-border collaboration in biotechnology and life sciences, Bengaluru-based Centre for Cellular and Molecular
articles.body: BENGALURU: In a move to strengthen cross-border collaboration in biotechnology and life sciences, Bengaluru-based Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP) has signed a partnership agreement with Genopole, France's biotechnology and genomics cluster.“The agreement was signed on the sidelines of Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, with Valérie Pécresse, president of the Île-de-France region, presiding over the ceremony. It envisages collaboration in research translation, technology transfers, entrepreneurship and access to funding opportunities in India and France,” C-CAMP said.The partnership will focus on areas including synthetic biology, genomics and biotechnology. It also proposes a pilot startup exchange programme that will offer entrepreneurs from both ecosystems opportunities for immersion, mentoring, access to curated investor networks and state-of-the-art research facilities.The two organisations will also explore exchanges of startup and technology portfolios to facilitate international incubation, establish launchpads for market entry and support the commercialisation of technologies.“The agreement provides for exploring joint funding opportunities through existing Indo-French govt collaborations, including the CEFIPRA/IFCPAR programme, as well as upcoming European Union programmes such as Horizon Europe,” C-CAMP said.C-CAMP director and CEO Taslimarif Saiyed said the partnership would seek to advance both deep science and impact-driven science translation, enabling technologies with applications in India and France. He said this was the organisation's second collaboration with the French innovation ecosystem, following an earlier partnership with Paris Santé.Genopole director-general David Bodet said both ecosystems faced challenges relating to high manufacturing costs and the ability to scale production to industrial levels. Combining expertise, he said, could help researchers and entrepreneurs address these constraints.The collaboration will seek to support the development of new therapies and technologies while also exploring biotechnology applications in industrial decarbonisation and environmental transition.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Bombay HC quashes ICICI Bank’s sanction to prosecute ex-CEO Chanda Kochhar
articles.summary: Bombay High Court on Wednesday set aside ICICI Bank’s sanction to prosecute its former CEO Chanda Kochhar in connection with alleged irregularities in
articles.body: Bombay High Court on Wednesday set aside ICICI Bank’s sanction to prosecute its former CEO Chanda Kochhar in connection with alleged irregularities in loans extended to the videocon group, led by Venugopal Dhoot.According to news agency PTI, a single-judge bench of justice Milind Jadhav ruled that the authority granting the sanction had failed to apply its mind to the material placed before it.“The impugned sanction dated May 15, 2023, is illegal and deserves to be quashed on the ground that the authority that granted the same is not a competent authority and it completely failed to apply its mind to the material, or lack thereof, placed before it while granting sanction,” the court observed.The High Court said the sanction order was legally unsustainable and therefore null and void.The court delivered its verdict on a petition filed by Kochhar, who argued that ICICI Bank had not followed the prescribed procedure while approving the sanction for her prosecution.The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) arrested Kochhar and her husband, Deepak Kochhar, in December 2022 in connection with the alleged loan fraud. The couple received interim bail in January 2023.In June 2023, the CBI told a special court in Mumbai that ICICI Bank had approved the sanction to prosecute Kochhar because there appeared to be a quid pro quo, an exchange of favours in the loan extended to videocon.Such approval is mandatory under the prevention of corruption act because bank employees are treated as public servants under the law.The case relates to a Rs 3,250-crore loan that ICICI Bank sanctioned to the videocon group in 2012, when Kochhar was at the helm of the bank. The CBI has alleged cheating and irregularities in the loan approval process.According to the investigating agency, Kochhar cleared the loan because her husband and family members stood to benefit from the transaction. In return, videocon allegedly invested in Nu renewable, a company linked to her husband, the CBI has claimed.The loan later turned into a non-performing asset (NPA) and was classified as a bank fraud case.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: SpiceJet board approves Rs 5,500 crore fundraise plan to revive cash-strapped airline
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cash-strapped budget airline SpiceJet has approved a proposal to raise up to Rs 5,500 crore to strengthen its finances, rebuild its fleet and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cash-strapped budget airline SpiceJet has approved a proposal to raise up to Rs 5,500 crore to strengthen its finances, rebuild its fleet and support its revival.The airline's board cleared the fundraising plan at a meeting on Wednesday, after being briefed on investment discussions with potential new investors. The proposed capital raise will be carried out through a combination of equity and other permitted instruments, subject to the necessary shareholder and regulatory approvals, SpiceJet said in a statement.The board has also approved a proposal to increase the company's authorised share capital from Rs 2,000 crore to Rs 7,500 crore, subject to the required approvals. It has directed the management to expedite the fundraising process.The move comes as SpiceJet faces mounting pressure on its operations and finances. Its domestic market share fell to 0.6% in September from 1.2% in August, according to the latest data from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA).The airline attributed the strain to geopolitical disruptions and airspace restrictions, alongside a sharp rise in aviation turbine fuel (ATF) prices, which it said had more than doubled over the past few months. The proposed fundraise is expected to provide funds to strengthen its balance sheet, support fleet expansion and meet operational requirements.Fleet expansion plans amid financial pressureSpiceJet has been working to expand its operational fleet even as it struggles with aircraft groundings, payment pressures and a cash crunch. The airline had announced in September that it had finalised lease agreements with three aircraft operators to induct 20 planes ahead of the winter schedule.The planned additions comprise 15 Boeing and five Airbus aircraft under damp and wet lease arrangements, with phased induction scheduled between mid-October and mid-November.The airline had earlier outlined plans to increase operations to around 200 daily flights during the winter schedule, with higher frequencies on key routes and expanded domestic and international connectivity. It currently operates around nine aircraft from its own fleet, alongside a number of wet-leased planes.SpiceJet had also received Rs 150 crore under the Centre's Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS), the government said in September, adding that the aviation regulator was monitoring the airline's operations and financial position.The carrier is also facing legal and payment-related challenges, including insolvency petitions filed by lessors and claims involving former promoter Kalanithi Maran and KAL Airways.SpiceJet chairman and managing director Ajay Singh said the proposed fundraising would provide an opportunity to rebuild the airline, strengthen operations and restore the brand.Shares of SpiceJet rose nearly 5% to Rs 9.97 apiece in late afternoon trade on the BSE on Wednesday.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic and other global AI firms expand in India as 24 overseas tech companies grow their combined workforce by over 30% to 24,000, with mid-career talent driving demand
articles.summary: There is a growing demand for India’s talent as global artificial intelligence (AI) and technology firms are turning to the country in greater numbers to
articles.body: There is a growing demand for India’s talent as global artificial intelligence (AI) and technology firms are turning to the country in greater numbers to recruit talent and develop products, with startups and mid-sized companies increasingly relying on the country’s engineers for product research and development.Despite India's large pool of engineers, competition for skilled professionals is intense, with domestic and international startups competing against IT services companies, global capability centres (GCCs) and businesses in other sectors, industry experts said.Kapil Joshi, CEO of IT staffing and IT solutions at Quess Corp, said professionals with four to 12 years of experience, capable of implementing AI solutions and taking projects into production, make up 55% of total demand.Growing demand for India’s talentA group of 24 international AI and emerging technology companies, excluding Big Tech, tracked by staffing firm Xpheno, expanded their combined employee strength in India by over 30% in the past year to approximately 24,000.The companies span several segments, including AI, robotics, cybersecurity, fintech and enterprise software. The list includes Anthropic, OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Perplexity, Replit, Wispr Flow, Databricks, Figma, Rippling, Harness and Glean.“India may not be comparable to Silicon Valley today in terms of the depth of its AI talent, but it has the potential,” Kamal Karanth, cofounder of Xpheno told ET.Pointing to the increasing number of emerging technology companies recruiting in India, he said, “From a future investment perspective, companies want to build that capability here.”The US has produced nearly 200 unicorns over the past two years, and many of these companies have access to talent in India, Karanth said.Industry executives, including founders, staffing firms and analysts, attributed the trend to several factors.These include the growing ability of Indian teams to build and customise technology products for global markets, as well as the challenges of recruiting talent in established technology centres such as San Francisco. These factors are prompting international technology companies to establish teams in India and expand their existing operations.Companies such as Rippling and Databricks are primarily interested in India’s engineering workforce, while ElevenLabs and Wispr Flow are expanding locally to serve their growing user base in the country, said Pratyush Choudhury, cofounder and general partner at AI-focused venture fund Activate.“For ElevenLabs and Wispr Flow, India became an important market early on…and they need local teams to adapt and customise their products for Indian users and customers ,” he said. India ranks as the second- or third-largest market outside the US for both companies, he added.Activate invests in early-stage startups working across AI applications, foundational models and infrastructure. Its portfolio includes both ElevenLabs and Wispr Flow.Choudhury, who also works closely with startups on recruitment, pointed to Wispr Flow’s Android product to illustrate how the Indian market has shaped product requirements. The need to address keyboard functionality and mobile usage became apparent as the company catered to Indian users.ElevenLabs, meanwhile, collaborated with Indian startups on developing models and sourcing data to train them.Manav Garg, former executive chairman of Emergent Labs, said the growing presence of founders and senior executives of Indian origin in Silicon Valley is also helping international startups establish operations in India. Garg is launching an agentic commerce startup backed by Flipkart and Navi cofounder Sachin Bansal.“The Indian diaspora in Silicon Valley has a better understanding of the local talent market and can leverage its connections to build teams here,” Garg said.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Scotch on the rocks? India imposes 162.5% duty, tax on bulk UK imports; domestic production likely to be hit
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India is imposing an effective duty and tax of 162.5 per cent on bulk Scotch whisky imports from Britain, higher than the 150 per cent levied
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India is imposing an effective duty and tax of 162.5 per cent on bulk Scotch whisky imports from Britain, higher than the 150 per cent levied before the India-UK trade agreement came into force, according to a Reuters report. This comes amid a dispute over customs classification.The higher levy has put liquor companies, including Pernod Ricard and Diageo, in a difficult position, with more than 80 containers of bulk Scotch belonging to Pernod, Diageo and Bacardi reportedly stuck at Indian ports.Under the India-UK trade agreement, implemented on July 15, New Delhi agreed to reduce import duty on certain Scotch whisky products from 150 per cent to 75 per cent.The reduction was welcomed by British exporters and liquor companies that import Scotch in bulk and blend it with Indian spirits to manufacture popular whisky brands.However, it was found that the companies were using incorrect customs classifications for bulk Scotch imports, which are used as raw material in blended whisky production.According to the Reuters report, investigators have said that such imports fall under a new customs classification introduced in May for "compound alcoholic preparations", which attracts a 150 per cent customs duty. An additional consumption tax takes the effective levy to 162.5 per cent, according to a government document reviewed by Reuters.The liquor companies maintain that both bulk and bottled Scotch imports should qualify for the reduced 75 per cent duty under the trade agreement.With the investigation under way, authorities have allowed provisional release of the consignments. Under the arrangement, companies must pay duty equivalent to 75 per cent of the goods' value upfront, while the remaining amount is to be secured through bank guarantees, Reuters reported.Pernod Ricard and Diageo have moved to arrange bank guarantees and other funding to secure the release of their consignments, while Bacardi is still considering its options, according to the report.The higher levy has also raised concerns over possible disruptions to domestic whisky production. Mumbai-listed liquor companies Radico Khaitan, Allied Blenders and Distillers, and Tilaknagar Industries, which also import bulk Scotch, are among those under scrutiny.Smaller companies could face greater financial pressure in arranging bank guarantees, particularly if collateral is required. Such guarantees also have to be reported as contingent liabilities.A liquor industry executive told Reuters that companies had little alternative but to arrange the guarantees, as maintaining production was critical, despite the pressure on working capital.Around 80 per cent of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume arrive in bulk, according to industry estimates. India is the largest market for Scotch whisky by export volume.Most bulk imports are used to manufacture Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) whisky by blending Scotch with other spirits. These products are generally sold at lower prices than fully imported brands such as Chivas Regal and Johnnie Walker.The dispute has also drawn the attention of the British government, which has repeatedly said it is working with New Delhi to resolve the issue and ensure British businesses can export under the tariff terms agreed in the trade pact.India has said the matter will be resolved soon. However, a confidential memo by Indian investigators, reported by Reuters, said any misclassification under the India-UK agreement must stop, citing "substantial revenue implications" for the government.The Scotch Whisky Association has estimated that the trade agreement could increase Scotch exports to India by $1.34 billion over five years.The additional consumption tax has come as a surprise to the liquor industry, with one industry source describing the move to Reuters as a "googly".Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: First customers, not just funding, key hurdle for deeptech startups
articles.summary: Indian deeptech startups in materials and semiconductors struggle to secure first commercial orders; founders urge govt procurement, partnerships and manufacturing support.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Indian deeptech startups developing advanced materials and semiconductors face a major challenge in securing their first commercial orders, even as access to venture capital improves, founders said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on Wednesday.Hareesh Chandrasekar, co-founder of AGNIT Semiconductors, which develops gallium nitride-based semiconductor wafers and chips, said winning initial orders was often harder than developing the technology itself.“How does the government become the first customer?” he asked, adding that deploying the first 10,000-20,000 chips would help Indian manufacturers establish credibility with global buyers.He said govt agencies and large Indian companies needed to take greater chances on domestic technologies. AGNIT has been shipping wafers to international customers and is expanding its chip manufacturing business.Gadhadar Reddy, founder of NoPo Nanotechnologies, which manufactures carbon nanotubes used in batteries and semiconductors, highlighted difficulties in setting up manufacturing facilities, including navigating multiple approvals.Murari Ramkumar, founder of Vimano, which develops advanced membranes for hydrogen and energy-storage applications, said startups must compete with established technologies on both cost and durability.Siddharth Jena, founder of Akashalabdhi Space, which is developing materials-manufacturing capabilities in orbit, said scaling laboratory processes to industrial production remained a significant challenge.Kajal Shah, co-founder of battery technology startup Dreamfly Innovations, stressed the importance of extensive testing before commercial deployment, particularly for demanding applications such as drones.The founders said India needed stronger industry partnerships, early procurement commitments and manufacturing support to help research-led companies become globally competitive businesses.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Anthropic’s registered trademark does not rule out passing-off claim: Lawyer
articles.summary: Belagavi firm says lawsuit vs US-based Anthropic can proceed as a passing-off claim without a registered trademark; court to hear reply Nov 23.
articles.body: Belagavi: Belagavi-based Anthropic Softwares has argued before the Belagavi District Commercial Court that its suit against US-based AI company Anthropic is maintainable even though it does not have a registered trademark.The argument follows the defendant’s contention at the previous hearing that the suit was not maintainable without a registered trademark. The defence had also questioned the jurisdiction of the Belagavi Commercial Court.Appearing for the plaintiff on Tuesday, advocate M M Sheikh argued that the dispute concerns passing off rather than trademark infringement. While an infringement claim generally requires a registered trademark, a passing-off action can be brought even without registration, he submitted.He argued that the plaintiff was entitled to seek legal protection where the cause of action arose. He also contended that registration of a trademark does not give a company the right to exploit another business’s established goodwill or automatically protect it from a passing-off action.He submitted that Anthropic Softwares had built its reputation through years of investment and business development, and alleged that the defendant was attempting to exploit the goodwill of the Belagavi-based company.“The Anthropic Softwares company was registered in 2017 and has remained operational since then. It has invested considerable resources, time and effort to nurture this business like a child. Now, a foreign entity is attempting to destroy it. Such exploitation must be restrained,” he argued.Referring to Section 27(2) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, Sheikh said it preserves the right to initiate passing-off proceedings irrespective of whether a trademark is registered. He argued that Sections 28 and 29, cited by the defendant, deal with rights arising from trademark registration and infringement of registered trademarks, respectively.Countering the defendant’s contention that Anthropic India Pvt Ltd, Bengaluru, was a separate legal entity from its US-based parent, Sheikh said the Indian company was a subsidiary and that its relationship with the parent should be considered in the dispute.On jurisdiction, he referred to Sections 15 and 21 of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, arguing that intellectual property disputes, including those involving trademarks and domain names, qualify as commercial disputes under the Act.The defendant’s counsel sought time to file a brief reply to the allegations. Judge R P Gowda adjourned the matter to Nov 23.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: Sovereign capital pool nears Rs 2 lakh cr: Govt
articles.summary: Nearly Rs 2 lakh crore in sovereign capital is available for India’s startup ecosystem; govt plans long-term AIFs and RDI loans to boost deeptech.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Nearly Rs 2 lakh crore in sovereign capital is available across central and state govt funding initiatives, a senior govt official said on Wednesday, urging India’s venture capital industry to build larger funds and step up investments in deeptech startups.“If I combine the total fund which is moving from the central government and the state governments, almost Rs 2 lakh crore is available as a sovereign capital to the ecosystem,” said SP Singh, nodal officer in charge of the Centre’s Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund, at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 on Wednesday.Singh also disclosed plans for a govt-backed alternative investment fund (AIF) that could remain invested in deeptech companies for 25 years. He said the RDI Fund was designed to offer long-term loans at zero or ultra-low interest rates, reducing the need for startups to dilute ownership at an early stage.Naganand Doraswamy, founder and managing partner of Ideaspring Capital, flagged the mismatch between traditional venture capital investment cycles and the needs of deeptech companies.He said deeptech businesses often needed 12-15 years to mature, while many investors were reluctant to lock up capital beyond four or five years. “That is still the mindset that people have as LPs in India,” he said, referring to investors in venture funds.Arijit Dutt, chief general manager at SIDBI, said the Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 had a dedicated allocation for deeptech-focused funds, allowing fund lifespans of up to 15 years. Govt commitments could cover up to 25% of a fund’s corpus, capped at Rs 500 crore.“We also want to see some funds investing in early stage startups,” Dutt said, adding that much of the current interest was concentrated in Series B and later-stage companies where initial technology risks had been reduced.In his keynote, Accel India founding partner Prashanth Prakash said Indian startups had an opportunity to develop critical technologies for global markets, particularly in defence, cybersecurity, communications and AI.“India can move from being a buyer of sovereign technology to becoming a global supplier of sovereign capabilities,” he said. Prakash cited defence technology company Constelli, which began by developing radar and electronic warfare solutions for Indian customers before expanding internationally, as an example of this opportunity.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: APTEL issues notices to HERC, Haryana govt in Eleven Power case
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) on Wednesday directed Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission (HERC) and Haryana govt to file
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) on Wednesday directed Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission (HERC) and Haryana govt to file their replies within two weeks on an appeal challenging the decision to withhold the implementation of a distribution licence granted to Eleven Power for Gurugram and Nuh.The matter will come up for further hearing on Dec 2.HERC had on Oct 19 allowed a 25-year licence to be granted to Medanta co-founder Sunil Sachdeva–led Eleven Power Private Ltd (EPPL) for setting up a parallel power distribution network in the two Haryana districts under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003, which permits more than one distribution company to operate in the same area. The licence covered Gurugram City, Gurugram Sub-urban, Manesar, Sohna and Nuh, with electricity supply expected to begin in FY2027-28.The Haryana govt, however, invoked Section 108(1) of the Act and asked the power regulator on Oct 26 not to “create, operationalise or effectuate” a parallel distribution licence anywhere in the state. Acting on the directives, HERC issued an order on Oct 28, saying it had decided not to proceed further with the matter, while rejecting EPPL’s request for advance notice and a hearing on any proceedings concerning the licence. Section 108(1) requires state electricity commissions to be guided by govt directives on policy matters involving public interest.During Wednesday’s hearing, APTEL directed the respondents to file their replies within two weeks, following which rejoinders will be filed ahead of the next hearing.An Eleven Power spokesperson said the company remained certain of its position and was committed to pursuing the matter through due process, while continuing to focus on delivering reliable power distribution services to consumers in Gurugram and Nuh.Money habits form by age 7.
